author: Austen
context: a wealthy single man is assumed to want a wife
masterwork: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
plain: Everyone agrees that a rich unmarried man probably wants to find a wife.

author: Dickens
context: the era was simultaneously good and bad
masterwork: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.
plain: The period was both very good and very bad at once.

author: Melville
context: the true place cannot be found on any map
masterwork: It is not down in any map; true places never are.
plain: You won't find it on a map, because real places never appear on maps.

author: Tolstoy
context: happy families are alike while unhappy ones differ
masterwork: Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
plain: All happy families are similar, but each unhappy family is unhappy differently.

author: Kafka
context: a man wakes to find he has become a giant insect
masterwork: As Gregor Samsa awoke one morning from uneasy dreams he found himself transformed in his bed into a gigantic insect.
plain: One morning Gregor Samsa woke from bad dreams and found he had turned into a huge insect in his bed.

author: Thoreau
context: he moved to the woods to live deliberately
masterwork: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life.
plain: I moved to the forest because I wanted to live on purpose and face only what mattered.

author: Dickens
context: the book will reveal who the hero of his life is
masterwork: Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life, or whether that station will be held by anybody else, these pages must show.
plain: Whether I become the main figure of my own life or someone else does, this book will show.

author: Melville
context: the narrator gives his name as Ishmael
masterwork: Call me Ishmael.
plain: You can call me Ishmael.

author: Dickinson
work: Because I could not stop for Death
source_url: canonical:Because I could not stop for Death
context: death waited for the speaker who had no time
masterwork: Because I could not stop for Death, He kindly stopped for me.
plain: Since I had no time to stop for death, it politely stopped for me.

author: Dickinson
work: Hope is the thing with feathers
source_url: canonical:Hope is the thing with feathers
context: hope is like a bird living in the soul
masterwork: Hope is the thing with feathers that perches in the soul.
plain: Hope is like a bird that sits inside the spirit.

author: Frost
context: he chose the less-traveled of two paths
masterwork: Two roads diverged in a wood, and I took the one less traveled by.
plain: Two paths split in the forest, and I chose the less-used one.

author: Frost
context: the woods are lovely but he has duties
masterwork: The woods are lovely, dark and deep, but I have promises to keep.
plain: The forest is beautiful and dark, but I have obligations to fulfill.

author: Whitman
context: the speaker cries out loudly over the world
masterwork: I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world.
plain: I shout loudly and wildly out across the whole world.

author: Blake
context: seeing the world in a grain of sand, heaven in a flower
masterwork: To see a World in a Grain of Sand and a Heaven in a Wild Flower.
plain: To find the whole world in one grain of sand and heaven in a wildflower.

author: Keats
context: beautiful things bring lasting joy
masterwork: A thing of beauty is a joy for ever.
plain: A beautiful thing brings happiness that lasts forever.

author: Shelley
context: the powerful should look at his works and despair
masterwork: Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
plain: Powerful people, look at what I built and lose hope.

author: Tennyson
context: loving and losing beats never loving
masterwork: 'Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all.
plain: It is better to have loved and lost someone than to never have loved.

author: Hopkins
context: the world is filled with divine grandeur
masterwork: The world is charged with the grandeur of God.
plain: The world is full of God's greatness.

author: Coleridge
work: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
source_url: canonical:The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
context: surrounded by water, yet none is drinkable
masterwork: Water, water, every where, nor any drop to drink.
plain: There was water all around, but none of it could be drunk.

author: Shakespeare
context: comparing the beloved favorably to a summer day
masterwork: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? Thou art more lovely and more temperate.
plain: Should I compare you to a summer day? You are lovelier and milder.

author: Shakespeare
context: life is a brief, poor performance on a stage
masterwork: Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player that struts and frets his hour upon the stage.
plain: Life is only a moving shadow, a bad actor who nervously performs his brief time on stage.

author: Dickinson
context: a nobody asks whether the reader is also a nobody
masterwork: I'm Nobody! Who are you? Are you Nobody too?
plain: I am unimportant. Who are you? Are you unimportant as well?

author: Donne
context: no one exists in total isolation
masterwork: No man is an island, entire of itself.
plain: No person is completely separate and self-sufficient.

author: Marvell
context: if there were sufficient time and space
masterwork: Had we but world enough, and time.
plain: If only we had enough space and time.

author: Wordsworth
context: the speaker wandered alone like a cloud
masterwork: I wandered lonely as a cloud that floats on high o'er vales and hills.
plain: I walked around by myself like a cloud drifting over valleys and hills.

author: Poe
context: late at night the tired speaker sat thinking
masterwork: Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary.
plain: Late one gloomy night, while I was thinking, tired and worn out.

author: Yeats
context: things disintegrate and cannot hold together
masterwork: Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold.
plain: Everything breaks down; the middle can't stay together.

author: Eliot
context: he has parceled his life into tiny measures
masterwork: I have measured out my life with coffee spoons.
plain: I have counted out my life in small dull routines.

author: Wilde
context: all are low, but some still look upward
masterwork: We are all in the gutter, but some of us are looking at the stars.
plain: We are all in a low situation, but some of us stay hopeful.

author: Wilde
context: the speaker resists all but temptation
masterwork: I can resist everything except temptation.
plain: I can resist anything except things that tempt me.

author: Twain
context: rumors of his death were overstated
masterwork: The reports of my death have been greatly exaggerated.
plain: The news that I had died was very inaccurate.

author: Thoreau
context: most people live in quiet despair
masterwork: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
plain: Most people live lives of silent unhappiness.

author: Emerson
context: greatness brings being misunderstood
masterwork: To be great is to be misunderstood.
plain: Being great means that people will not understand you.

author: Franklin
context: only death and taxes are certain
masterwork: In this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes.
plain: The only certain things in life are dying and paying taxes.

author: Bacon
context: books deserve different depths of reading
masterwork: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested.
plain: Some books you sample, some you read quickly, and a few you study carefully.

author: Shakespeare
context: the question of whether to live or die
masterwork: To be, or not to be, that is the question.
plain: Whether to keep living or to die is the question.
